question: How should nuclear waste and long-lived spent fuel be safely managed?
summary: Commercial nuclear power produces small physical volumes of high-level waste (HLW) per unit of electricity generated, but that waste remains radiotoxic for hundreds of thousands of years. Consensus centers on deep geological repositories (DGRs) for permanent isolation, while interim dry-cask storage safely bridges decades of operational waiting.

arguments.title: Compact physical volume allows comprehensive containment
arguments.body: Because of uranium's extreme energy density, the total high-level waste generated by an individual's lifetime of all-nuclear electricity fits within a single soda can (~250-300 grams). Unlike fossil effluents, all commercial high-level nuclear waste is captured, solid, accountably tracked, and contained rather than released into the biosphere.

arguments.title: Deep geological repositories are technically viable and licensed
arguments.body: Finland's Onkalo repository at Olkiluoto has received regulatory construction and operating approval to entomb copper-canistered spent fuel 400+ meters deep in two-billion-year-old stable crystalline bedrock, demonstrating that deep geological disposal is an engineered reality rather than an unsolved theoretical challenge.

arguments.title: Extreme radiotoxic lifespans create political stalemates and intergenerational burdens
arguments.body: Transuranic actinides such as Plutonium-239 and Americium-241 remain radiotoxic for over 100,000 years, requiring institutional stability, warning markers, and geological isolation that outlast recorded human civilization. Political opposition (NIMBYism) has derailed repositories in the United States (Yucca Mountain) and elsewhere for decades.

arguments.title: Decades of safe dry-cask storage provide operational buffer
arguments.body: After 5 to 10 years in cooling pools, spent fuel can be passively cooled in helium-filled steel and reinforced concrete dry storage casks. Decades of operational experience across hundreds of installations demonstrate zero radiological leakage and high resilience to extreme natural disasters.

arguments.title: Reprocessing and fast breeder recycling extract energy but add proliferation complexity
arguments.body: Closed fuel cycles (e.g. in France at La Hague, and in Russia) separate unspent uranium and plutonium, reducing high-level waste volume by ~75% and radiotoxicity lifespan from 100,000 to ~1,000 years. However, chemical reprocessing introduces separation steps, proliferation safeguards overhead, and high capital processing costs.

consensus.statement: There is broad international consensus among geological surveys, nuclear regulators (STUK, NRC), and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency that deep geological disposal in stable rock formations (granite, clay, or salt) is technically sound and passively safe over multi-millennial timescales.
consensus.basis: OECD-NEA Global Status Assessment and STUK licensing evaluations

uncertainty.statement: The primary barrier to deep geological repository deployment remains democratic political consent and local site licensing rather than hydrological or material engineering feasibility.
uncertainty.basis: IAEA and NEA socio-technical governance reviews across member states

missingEvidenceNote: Empirical long-term corrosion rates of engineered barrier canisters (copper, nickel alloy) rely on accelerated electrochemical testing and natural analogues (e.g. Oklo natural reactors), which carry small model uncertainty over 100,000-year periods.
